deep.reconstruction:
The page contains no mathematical derivation. Its only content is a small pen sketch map drawn on a graticule of whole degrees. The vertical axis is labelled 40, 41, 42, 43, 44, with values increasing downward, so these are southern latitudes. The horizontal axis is labelled 144, 145, 146, 147, 148, 149, which are eastern longitudes. Some longitude labels look overwritten or corrected (the first may read 144 written over 143, and 145 and 146 are retouched).

The outline inside the grid fits Tasmania (Van Diemen's Land), as do its position and shape:
- North-west corner near 40.7°S, 144.7°E (Cape Grim region).
- North coast running east to the north-east tip near 40.8°S, 148.3°E.
- West coast falling south-east to about 145.5°E at 42–43°S.
- Southern coast near 43.6–43.7°S around 146–147°E (South East Cape about 146.8°E).
- East coast near 148°E, with the small looped appendage at about 43°S, 147.6–148°E. This loop matches the Forestier and Tasman Peninsulas joined by a narrow neck, enclosing Norfolk Bay and Frederick Henry Bay.

The drawing is a simple plate carrée (equirectangular) plot of coastline points read from some source map or coordinate list. No computation is shown.

Context (my inference, not on the page): a likely motive is Gauss's terrestrial-magnetism work around 1838–1845. The Ross Antarctic expedition and the magnetic observatory at Hobarton, Van Diemen's Land (about 42.9°S, 147.3°E), were part of the Göttingen Magnetic Union / British Magnetic Crusade network. Gauss may have wanted to locate Hobarton or the island when handling magnetic data. This is plausible but not certain.

The previous page, a table of primes 829–997 with marks (apparently quadratic-residue relations), is unrelated to this sketch.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no derivation.

Cartographically, the grid cells are drawn nearly square. At about 42°S a degree of longitude is only about cos(42°) ≈ 0.74 of a degree of latitude, so the island is stretched east–west relative to a conformal or true-scale rendering. This is harmless for a locational sketch.
The coastline is generalized: the sketch puts the southern extremity near 43.8°S, slightly south of the true ~43.64°S.

results.what: Sketch map of Tasmania on a 1° latitude/longitude graticule (40–44°S, 144–149°E)
results.usually_credited_to: Ancient (Marinus of Tyre / Ptolemy for the projection); coastline data from British and French surveys of Van Diemen's Land (Flinders, Baudin expedition, etc.)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a simple geographic sketch of Tasmania with no mathematical content. Gauss's interest in global geography and in the southern magnetic stations (e.g. Hobarton) is well known, so a locational sketch is unremarkable.

checkable.asserts: The east–west scale factor at 42°S is about 0.743, showing the nearly square grid cells exaggerate longitude spacing.
Tasmania's extremal coordinates (about 40.68–43.64°S, 144.6–148.4°E) lie within the drawn graticule 40–44°S, 144–149°E.

transcription_corrections: The first longitude label is probably '144' written over another digit (possibly 143). The labels '145' and '146' are also overwritten or corrected in the manuscript.
The latitude labels 40–44 increase downward and so denote southern latitudes. The bracketed description could be made specific: '[Sketch map of Van Diemen's Land / Tasmania on a 1° grid]'.
